title: Spatial Buffer & Overlay Analyzer
description: Run buffer and overlay analysis with the Spatial Buffer & Overlay Analyzer — what's within X miles, and what exactly is in there. Free.
summary_sentence: A 72-point spherical circle and capped OSM node counts provide a preliminary approximation.
quick_answer: Choose a centre and a 1–50 mile radius to draw an approximate circle and count up to 2,000 returned OSM city, town, village, school and hospital nodes. Ways and relations are excluded; results are not complete or official.
steps_intro: Buffer draws the circle; overlay counts its contents:

body.t: Candidate sites compared by what their buffers contain — population proxies, facilities, competitors' absence. The
'Within 2 miles of the proposed site lie 3 schools and a hospital' is a buffer-overlay sentence — this tool produces it with the arithmetic shown.
Protected sites, water features and settlements within a works radius — the screening every assessment opens with.
Buffer and overlay are the two verbs of spatial analysis. This page lets students perform both before they meet the software that industrialises them.
Doubling the radius from 2 to 4 miles quadruples the buffered ground (12.6 → 50.3 sq mi) — and roughly quadruples everything counted in it. Radius choices are never casual.

A facility just outside the line is outside — overlay counts containment, not closeness. The professional habit is to report a second, wider buffer alongside, so edge sensitivity is visible rather than hidden.

popular_table.title: Buffer sizes and their ground
popular_table.intro: The area each radius commands — the denominator of every count.
popular_table.note: Counts come from open map data (towns, schools, hospitals as recorded) — deep in mapped regions, thinner where mapping is sparse; the page reports the data's answer, not the world's census.

faq: Only returned OSM nodes with the selected tags are counted, with a combined limit of 2,000. Ways, relations and unmapped features are excluded.
Buffer around a point or a shape?
This analyzer buffers a centre point; buffers around lines and polygons are full-GIS operations built on the same principle.
The analysis reports counts for the study; the underlying places are the map's own records, explorable on the linked tools.
Run separately, each buffer counts its own contents — a place between two sites appears in both studies, correctly for site comparison.
A refinement: equal-time shapes bend with roads. The circular buffer is the screening standard because it is reproducible by anyone, anywhere.
How big a radius is sane?
The radius control is limited to 1–50 miles. The area shown uses the planar πr² approximation.
Run each centre and compare tables — systematic comparison is the method; the tool keeps each run clean.
